name: gt
popularity: 141 stars, 39 forks, 13 watchers. Backed by ao-space (a Chinese open-source personal cloud project), used as part of that ecosystem; not widely adopted outside it.
maturity: Actively maintained (86 commits, dev branch, CI via GitHub Actions, tagged releases with prebuilt binaries and Docker images for both server/client). No red flags found; project is fairly young but functional and receives updates.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN interface — it's a userspace WebSocket(s)/HTTP(s)/TCP relay proxy, not a VPN. No root/admin required. Simple: single static binary (`gt client`) or Docker image; zero-config startup opens a web admin UI to configure. Very low friction.
server_requirements: Server source fully available (Rust, same repo). Config-file-driven (YAML) with a bundled web configuration UI for setup, not a REST/programmatic API intended for external orchestration. No documented TypeScript/JS SDK.
has_programmable_api: false — the server exposes a browser-based web admin config UI (not a documented REST API) and is driven by YAML config files/CLI signals (reload/restart/stop); no TS/JS SDK found.
viability_notes: Meets all hard client constraints (no TUN, no root, single binary) and the hosted server binary model fits well (prebuilt release binaries + Docker images). Lacks a clean programmatic HTTP API for tunnel registration — would need to drive it via generated YAML config + reload signals from glue code. Good candidate if we're willing to shell out to config-file management.

name: docker-wireguard-tunnel
popularity: 116 stars, 14 forks, 3 watchers. Niche self-hosted homelab tool; no major notable adoption beyond GitHub stars.
maturity: 90 commits, active CI (build-and-push + check-for-updates workflows), latest tag v3, container images auto-published to GHCR. Actively maintained but small single-maintainer project.
client_requirements: DISQUALIFYING: requires an actual WireGuard kernel/userspace tunnel interface (wg0) and the container needs `cap_add: NET_ADMIN` to create it — this is a real VPN/TUN-based approach, not TUN-free. Requires Docker plus elevated network capability, effectively root-equivalent privileges on the host.
server_requirements: Source available (Dockerfile + shell scripts). Purely config-file/env-var driven (docker-compose environment variables like DOMAIN, PEERS, SERVICES); no HTTP control-plane or API for programmatic tunnel registration — peer configs are auto-generated as files.
has_programmable_api: false — purely docker-compose env/config file driven, no REST/JS API.
viability_notes: Confirmed WireGuard/TUN-based (NET_ADMIN capability, wg0 interface) which directly violates the no-TAP/TUN, no-admin/root client constraint. No programmable API either. Disqualified for this use case.

name: holepunch
popularity: 60 stars, 9 forks, 7 watchers. Was the backend for api.holepunch.io / holepunch.io ngrok-alternative product circa 2018-2019; modest historical visibility, not currently a live product as far as verifiable.
maturity: 83 commits, last significant activity appears old (CircleCI-era, Pipfile/pipenv, Python 3.7 pin) — codebase looks stale/abandoned. The README still references api.holepunch.io and holepunch.io as the live product; independent verification of current domain status was inconclusive via search, but the tooling (CircleCI, Codacy badges, Nomad/Grid deploy workflow, Python 3.7) strongly suggests the project and its hosted service are no longer actively maintained. Treat as likely defunct/stale — red flag for production use.
client_requirements: This repo is server-side only (Holepunch API/backend); the client is SSH-based (per README, tunnels are created via SSH remote port forwarding, similar to tnnlink) — no TAP/TUN, no special client software beyond an SSH client, so client-side is lightweight. However, no independent client binary in this repo to evaluate further.
server_requirements: Server source available (Flask app, Postgres migrations, Nomad/Docker deploy tooling via HashiCorp Nomad + Grid). It's a REST API (Flask, `rest-api` GitHub topic) but the deployment stack (Nomad cluster, custom VPN for deploy) is complex and clearly tailored to the original team's infra, not a portable turnkey server binary.
has_programmable_api: true — Flask REST API backend (Python) that provisions SSH-based reverse tunnels, but it is old, Nomad-cluster-dependent, and not packaged as a simple deployable binary/service.
viability_notes: Client side is admin-free/TUN-free (plain SSH), and it does have a REST API concept, but the project shows strong staleness signals (Python 3.7 pin, Nomad/Grid-specific deploy tooling, CircleCI-era stack) and heavy infra assumptions that make it impractical to stand up as a simple hosted server binary today. Low viability without significant modernization work.

name: specter
popularity: 48 stars, 1 fork, 4 watchers. Small but polished single-maintainer project ('like ngrok, but more ambitious with DHT for flavor'); no major notable third-party adoption found.
maturity: Very active: 729 commits, recent AGENTS.md/DESIGN.md/OPERATOR.md/PRODUCT.md docs suggest ongoing serious development, CI via GitHub Actions, requires Go 1.27.x and Node 22.12+ to build UI — modern toolchain, well-documented, no red flags.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN — client is a userspace Go binary using QUIC/TLS transport to tunnel L7 (HTTP/S) and L4 (TCP) traffic, including to Unix sockets/named pipes. No root/admin required. Simple YAML config or config-free `client expose`/`client serve` modes; single binary, cross-platform including macOS/Windows/Linux.
server_requirements: Full server source available (Go, self-hostable 'gateway' with Chord DHT overlay for routing, ACME/Let's Encrypt integration). Client offers a documented local management HTTP API/UI when started with `--server [host]:[port]` (manage custom hostnames, unpublish, release, list tunnels) — this is a management API on the CLIENT side, not the server's control-plane for creating tunnels; server itself is still primarily config/CLI driven (YAML apex config, gateway operator docs).
has_programmable_api: partial/true — Go-based local management API on the client (`--server` flag) for tunnel lifecycle operations; the gateway/server itself doesn't expose a documented public REST API for external registration, but is source-available and could be extended.
viability_notes: Excellent fit for the hard client constraints (no TUN, no root, single Go binary, even config-free modes) and the project is clearly actively engineered with strong docs. The programmable angle is only partial (client-side management API, not a full server control-plane), so registering tunnels programmatically from a SvelteKit backend would require either using the client API pattern or extending the Go server — feasible since source is available, but not a plug-and-play REST API out of the box.

name: wireport
popularity: 48 stars, 2 forks, 1 watcher. New project (video tutorial on YouTube), modest early traction, no major notable adoption yet.
maturity: 126 commits, actively developed, has GitHub Sponsors, releases for Linux/macOS/Windows on AMD64/ARM64. Reasonably fresh and maintained, but young project.
client_requirements: DISQUALIFYING: explicitly requires an installed WireGuard client and joins a real WireGuard VPN network (TUN interface) to reach the GATEWAY — README states 'Installed WireGuard client: required for connecting to the VPN tunnel.' This is a true VPN/TUN-based architecture, not TUN-free, and WireGuard setup typically needs elevated/admin privileges to create the interface.
server_requirements: Source available (Go + Caddy + CoreDNS + WireGuard stack). Configuration is via CLI commands and Docker labels for declarative tunnel config (not a documented HTTP REST API for external programmatic registration); described as a 'two commands' quick start rather than an API-first design.
has_programmable_api: false — CLI/docker-label driven, no documented REST/JS control-plane API.
viability_notes: Confirmed WireGuard/TUN-based client requirement, directly violating the hard no-TAP/TUN, no-admin constraint. No programmable API either. Disqualified for this use case despite otherwise solid engineering (SSL automation, service discovery).

name: YTunnel
popularity: 53 stars, 4 forks, 1 watcher. Small hobby/indie project (yetidevworks.com), no notable third-party adoption found.
maturity: 54 commits, has CHANGELOG.md, GitHub Actions CI, cargo/crates.io + Homebrew distribution — actively maintained, no obvious red flags, but it is a thin wrapper/management layer, not a full tunnel server implementation.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN. However it is fundamentally a management CLI/TUI wrapper around Cloudflare's `cloudflared` binary — requires installing cloudflared separately, a Cloudflare account, a domain managed by Cloudflare, and an API token with Zone/DNS/Tunnel edit permissions. Not root-required, but setup complexity is non-trivial (external SaaS dependency, DNS/API token config) and it does NOT let you run your own server — it relies entirely on Cloudflare's infrastructure as the 'server'.
server_requirements: DISQUALIFYING for our use case: there is no self-hostable server component at all — 'server' is Cloudflare's proprietary edge network via cloudflared. No option to run our own hosted server binary; fully dependent on Cloudflare's service and account model. Config is TOML files (config.toml, tunnels.toml), not a REST API we control.
server_language: N/A (relies on Cloudflare's closed infrastructure; cloudflared client only)
has_programmable_api: false — CLI/TOML config driven locally; it does call the Cloudflare API but that's a third-party SaaS API, not one we host.
viability_notes: Does not meet the core requirement of self-hosting our own server binary — it is entirely dependent on Cloudflare's proprietary tunnel infrastructure, which conflicts with 'we host it, source code preferred.' Client itself is fine (no TUN/root) but architecture is fundamentally wrong for this use case.

name: ngtor
popularity: 35 stars, 6 forks, 1 watcher. Niche/early-stage project, no notable adoption.
maturity: 91 commits, CI via GitHub Actions, tagged releases and Jitpack distribution. README explicitly states 'functional, but in early development. Expect breaking changes till v1.0 is reached.' — pre-1.0 stability risk flag.
client_requirements: Uses Tor as its transport — exposes local services as Tor hidden (.onion) services. No TAP/TUN interface, no root required (bundles tor-binary via bisq-network/tor-binary), single all-in-one JAR runnable with `java -jar ngtor.jar http --port=3000`. However inherent Tor overhead applies: high latency (multi-hop onion routing), variable/slow throughput, and .onion addresses instead of a normal custom domain — a significant functional/performance overhead flag for a general tunnel use case, plus requires Java >=21 runtime.
server_requirements: No traditional client/server split — ngtor IS both: it runs locally and publishes directly onto the Tor network (which acts as the 'relay'), so there's no separate hostable relay server component to control via an API. Fully CLI-driven, no REST/JS control-plane.
server_language: N/A (decentralized via Tor network itself; Java/Spring Boot app is the only component)
has_programmable_api: false — CLI only, Java/Spring Boot internals, no exposed control-plane API.
viability_notes: Tor-based architecture imposes major latency/overhead and produces .onion addresses rather than a normal reachable hostname, and there's no separate server component we host or control programmatically — it's architecturally mismatched with the hosted-server + control-plane requirement. Pre-1.0 stability caveat compounds the risk.

name: tnnlink
popularity: 26 stars, 6 forks, 0 watchers. Very small hobby project ('a fun weekend project'); the canonical repo has moved/renamed to github.com/faejr/tnnlink and is now archived.
maturity: DISQUALIFYING red flag: repository is archived (read-only) as of Jul 28, 2021 — only 9 commits total, explicitly marked by the author as unaudited and a first-time Go project. No maintenance for 4+ years; effectively abandoned.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN — client-side is just a standard SSH client doing remote port forwarding (`ssh <user>@host -p 2222 -R 80:localhost:<port>`), authenticated via GitHub public keys. No root/admin needed on client, no special install beyond an SSH client (already present on virtually all systems). This part is very lightweight.
server_requirements: Source available (small Go codebase, ~5 files). Purely config-file driven (single config.toml specifying HTTP/SSH ports, domain, SSL cert paths, GitHub-username whitelist) — no REST/HTTP control-plane or API for programmatic tunnel registration; tunnels are simply created ad hoc via SSH -R flags, not pre-registered through any API.
has_programmable_api: false — config.toml + SSH -R flags only, no API.
viability_notes: Archived/abandoned since 2021 with an explicit 'not audited' disclaimer from a self-described Go beginner — a clear maintenance/security red flag despite the appealingly lightweight SSH-based, TUN-free client model. Not viable to build on for a production hosted tunnel.
